kosmoceratops:eswiki:11.title: Kosmoceratops richardsoni (Función de la ornamentación del cráneo)

facts.statement: Fossils of Kosmoceratops were discovered in Utah within the Kaiparowits Formation during the years 2006 and 2007.
facts.quote: Specimens were discovered in Utah in the Kaiparowits Formation of the Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument in 2006 and 2007

facts.statement: The adult specimen was designated as the holotype for the new species Kosmoceratops richardsoni in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2010, the adult was made the holotype of the new genus and species Kosmoceratops richardsoni

facts.statement: The specific name 'richardsoni' honors Scott Richardson, the person who discovered the specimens.
facts.quote: the specific name honors Scott Richardson, who found the specimens

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops had an estimated length of 4.5 meters and a weight of 1.2 metric tons.
facts.quote: Kosmoceratops had an estimated length of 4.5 m and a weight of 1.2 MT

facts.statement: The horns of Kosmoceratops pointed upwards and to the sides before curving downwards to end in pointed tips.
facts.quote: the horns of Kosmoceratops pointed up and to the sides, then downwards, ending in pointed tips

facts.statement: The neck frill was short with small openings and featured ten hook-like structures on its back edge, eight of which curved forward and two curved to the sides.
facts.quote: The neck frill was short from front to back, with small parietal fenestrae (openings through the frill), and ten hook-like epiossifications on the hind margin, with eight curving forwards and two curving to the sides

facts.statement: The teeth of ceratopsids, including Kosmoceratops, were adapted for processing fibrous plants.
facts.quote: The teeth of ceratopsids were adapted to processing fibrous plants

facts.statement: Coprolites from the Kaiparowits Formation containing wood may have been produced by ceratopsids.
facts.quote: coprolites (fossilized dung) from the Kaiparowits Formation that contain wood may have been produced by ceratopsids

facts.statement: The functions of ceratopsian frills and horns are debated, with proposed roles including display, combat, and species recognition.
facts.quote: The functions of ceratopsian frills and horns have been debated, and include display, combat, and species recognition

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops is classified as a chasmosaurine ceratopsid.
facts.quote: Kosmoceratops was a chasmosaurine ceratopsid

facts.statement: The genus Kosmoceratops was described by Sampson et al. in 2010.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Sampson et al., 2010

facts.statement: The Kaiparowits Formation dates to the late Campanian age and was deposited on Laramidia, an island continent formed when North America was divided by the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: The Kaiparowits Formation dates to the late Campanian age and was deposited on Laramidia, an island continent, when North America was divided at the center by the Western Interior Seaway

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops was named in 2010 by paleontologist Scott D. Sampson and colleagues.
facts.quote: In 2010, the paleontologist Scott D. Sampson and colleagues named the new genus and species Kosmoceratops richardsoni, specimen UMNH VP 17000 (from Locality VP 890) being the holotype.

facts.statement: The species name richardsoni honors Scott Richardson, the volunteer who discovered the holotype.
facts.quote: The specific name honors Richardson, who found the holotype and many other fossils at GSENM.

facts.statement: The holotype was discovered by Scott Richardson during field seasons in 2006 and 2007.
facts.quote: Among the discoveries made were three new ceratopsian (horned dinosaur) taxa, one of which was identified from two localities (UMNH Locality VP 890 and 951) discovered by volunteer field crew member Scott Richardson during the field seasons of 2006 and 2007.

facts.statement: The full name Kosmoceratops richardsoni translates to "ornate horned face of Richardson".
facts.quote: The full name can be translated as "ornate horned face of Richardson".

facts.statement: The holotype skull is nearly complete but missing the predentary bone and parts of the left face and neck frill, with a snout bent to the right from postmortem distortion.
facts.quote: The holotype includes a nearly complete adult skull that is missing the predentary bone (the frontmost bone of the lower jaw) and a small part of the left side of the face and neck frill (parts of the jugal, squamosal, and parietal bones), and the snout is bent to the right due to postmortem (after death) distortion.

facts.statement: Four specimens of Kosmoceratops were reportedly found.
facts.quote: In all, four specimens were reportedly found.

facts.statement: James A. Campbell and colleagues rejected the assignment of specimen CMN 8801 to Kosmoceratops in 2016, arguing the features were likely due to taphonomy or variation within Chasmosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2016, the paleontologist James A. Campbell and colleagues did not support the assignment of specimen CMN 8801 to Kosmoceratops, as they found the features this was based on to be either influenced by taphonomy (changes occurring during decay and fossilization) or to fall within the variation among Chasmosaurus specimens (though they did not assign it to a particular species in the genus).

facts.statement: In 2020, Denver W. Fowler and Elizabeth A. Freedman Fowler suggested that specimen CMN 8801 might be reliably assigned to Kosmoceratops once the anatomy of chasmosaurine skull fronts is better understood.
facts.quote: In 2020, the paleontologists Denver W. Fowler and Elizabeth A. Freedman Fowler stated that CMN 8801 may be more reliably assigned when better understanding of the anatomy in the front part of chasmosaurine skulls is reached.

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops was estimated to reach a length of 4.5 meters and a weight of 1.2 metric tons.
facts.quote: Kosmoceratops is estimated to have been 4.5 m long and to have weighed 1.2 MT.

facts.statement: As a ceratopsid, Kosmoceratops was a quadruped with a heavily built skeleton, a large pelvis, and a relatively short tail.
facts.quote: As a ceratopsid, it would have been a quadruped with a heavily constructed skeleton, a large pelvis, and a relatively shortened tail.

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops possessed complex slicing dental batteries with hundreds of teeth located behind a toothless beak.
facts.quote: It had long main tooth rows which formed complex slicing dental batteries containing hundreds of teeth behind an edentulous (toothless) beak.

facts.statement: An alternate numbering system for Kosmoceratops' horn structures was proposed by Fowler and Fowler in 2020 based on comparisons with earlier Chasmosaurus species.
facts.quote: Fowler and Fowler proposed an alternate system in 2020, based on comparison with earlier Chasmosaurus species.

facts.statement: In 2010, researchers placed Kosmoceratops in the subfamily Chasmosaurinae based on skull features including a narial strut, a triangular process, and an elongated squamosal bone.
facts.quote: In 2010, Sampson and colleagues placed Kosmoceratops in the latter group due to the premaxilla having a narial strut and a triangular process, as well as the presence of an elongated squamosal bone.

facts.statement: Subsequent studies in 2011 and 2013 supported the grouping of Kosmoceratops and Vagaceratops together, though other researchers have argued for different relationships.
facts.quote: In 2011, the paleontologist Jordan C. Mallon and colleagues also found support for the clade containing Kosmoceratops and Vagaceratops, as did the paleontologists Steven L. Wick and Thomas M. Lehman in 2013.

facts.statement: In 2011, Denver Fowler and colleagues hypothesized that Kosmoceratops was an immature growth stage of Chasmosaurus irvinensis, suggesting its prominent skull ornamentation reduced with age.
facts.quote: In a 2011 conference abstract, the paleontologist Denver W. Fowler and colleagues suggested that many ceratopsid genera were merely ontogenetic morphs (or growth stages) of other genera and that Kosmoceratops was an immature stage of C. irvinensis (with the prominent skull ornamentation reducing with age).

facts.statement: In 2016, Jordan Mallon and colleagues found Kosmoceratops and Vagaceratops formed a clade with Spiclypeus as their sister taxon.
facts.quote: In 2016, Mallon and colleagues found Kosmoceratops and Vagaceratops to form a clade, with the new genus Spiclypeus as sister taxon.

facts.statement: In 2020, Denver Fowler and colleagues suggested a deep evolutionary split in chasmosaurines, finding Kosmoceratops closer to Chasmosaurus than previously thought.
facts.quote: In 2020, Fowler and Fowler described two new chasmosaurine genera, and suggested the subfamily had a deep evolutionary split between a clade containing Chasmosaurus and its closest relatives, and Pentaceratops and its relatives.

facts.statement: Histological study of Kosmoceratops bones revealed a dense network of blood vessels and high osteocyte counts, indicating sustained rapid growth.
facts.quote: The bone tissue had a high number of osteocytes (bone cells) as well as a dense network of blood vessels, including radially oriented vascular canals (blood canals running towards the bone interior), indicating sustained rapid growth.

facts.statement: Bone microstructure evidence suggests Kosmoceratops had an elevated metabolism and was endothermic, similar to modern birds and mammals.
facts.quote: These features also indicate that ceratopsians had an elevated metabolism and were homeothermic and endothermic (or "warm-blooded"), like modern birds and mammals.

facts.statement: The absence of annual growth lines in Kosmoceratops bones suggests it could sustain growth year-round, possibly due to a more equitable southern climate compared to northern relatives.
facts.quote: The Kosmoceratops and Utahceratops bones sampled by Levitt did not show evidence of lines of arrested growth (annual growth lines), and compared with the ceratopsids Pachyrhinosaurus, Centrosaurus, and Einosaurus from further north which did have growth lines, this may indicate that bone growth reacted to climate and that Kosmoceratops and Utahceratops could sustain their growth throughout the year due to their more equitable southern climate.

facts.statement: Fossilized dung from the Kaiparowits Formation, potentially from Kosmoceratops, contained fragments of angiosperm wood, indicating a diet of woody browse.
facts.quote: In a 2017 Master's thesis, the paleontologist Nicole Marie Ridgwell described two coprolites (fossilized dung) from the Kaiparowits Formation which, due to their size, may have been produced by a member of one of three herbivorous dinosaur groups known from the formation: ceratopsians (including Kosmoceratops), hadrosaurs, or ankylosaurs (rarest of the three groups).

facts.statement: Coprolites attributed to Kosmoceratops contained traces of mollusc shells, arthropod cuticle, and lizard bone, suggesting these items were ingested along with plant material.
facts.quote: The coprolites also contained traces of mollusc shell, arthropod cuticle, and lizard bone that may have been ingested along with the plant material.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the different diets found in coprolites indicate niche partitioning among herbivores or seasonal variation in diet.
facts.quote: The different diets represented by the coprolites may indicate niche partitioning among the herbivores of the Kaiparowits Formation ecosystem, or that there was seasonal variation in diet.

facts.statement: The dominant hypothesis suggests that the bizarre skull features of ceratopsians like Kosmoceratops were used to enhance reproductive success.
facts.quote: the dominant hypothesis involves enhancing reproductive success

facts.statement: In 2011, Padian and Horner proposed that bizarre dinosaur structures were primarily for species recognition, dismissing combat or temperature control explanations.
facts.quote: In 2011, the paleontologists Kevin Padian and John R. Horner proposed that "bizarre structures" in dinosaurs (including horns, frills, domes, and crests) were primarily used for species recognition

facts.statement: In 2013, Hone and Naish criticized the species recognition hypothesis, noting that no living animals use such structures primarily for that purpose.
facts.quote: In 2013, the paleontologists David E. Hone and Darren Naish criticized the "species recognition hypothesis", arguing that no extant animals use such structures primarily for species recognition

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops possessed the most complex neck frill margin among ceratopsians, having the highest values of fractal dimensions.
facts.quote: Kosmoceratops had the highest values of fractal dimensions in its neck frill margin (followed by Styracosaurus, Diabloceratops, and Centrosaurus)

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops lived in Utah between 76.4 and 75.5 million years ago during the late Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Kosmoceratops is known from the Kaiparowits Formation of Utah, which dates to the late Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous epoch, and occurs in a stratigraphic range spanning the upper part of its lower unit to the upper part of its middle unit, in sediments dating to 76.4–75.5 million years ago

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops inhabited a wet, humid environment featuring deep river channels, swamps, ponds, and lakes.
facts.quote: The formation represents an alluvial to coastal plain setting that was wet, humid, and dominated by large, deep channels with stable banks and perennial wetland swamps, ponds, and lakes

facts.statement: The wetlands where Kosmoceratops lived were dominated by cypress trees up to 30 meters tall and various aquatic plants.
facts.quote: The swamps and wetlands were dominated by up to 30 m cypress trees, ferns, and aquatic plants including giant duckweed, water lettuce, and other floating angiosperms

facts.statement: Better-drained areas in Kosmoceratops' habitat featured forests of 10-20 meter dicot trees and palms with fern understories.
facts.quote: Better-drained areas were dominated by forests of up to 10-20 m dicot trees and occasional palms, with an understory including ferns

facts.statement: Drier areas of the habitat were dominated by conifers up to 30 meters tall with cycads and small bushes in the understory.
facts.quote: Well-drained areas further away from wet areas were dominated by conifers up to 30 m, with an understory comprising cycads, small dicot trees or bushes, and possibly ferns

facts.statement: Cerapods, including Kosmoceratops, made up about 14 percent of the large vertebrate fossils found in the Kaiparowits Formation.
facts.quote: The two most common groups of large vertebrates in the formation are hadrosaurs and ceratopsians (the latter representing about 14 percent of associated vertebrate fossils)

facts.statement: Evidence suggests a pond environment for the deposition of the broken bones of the subadult or adult specimen UMNH VP 21339.
facts.quote: Levitt reported that every bone of the assigned subadult or adult specimen UMNH VP 21339 appeared to have been broken before depositing, and its matrix is stacked siltstones and mudstones with minor sandstones, which suggests a pond environment

facts.statement: The boundary between northern and southern dinosaur provinces on Laramidia lay around modern northern Utah and Colorado.
facts.quote: the boundary lying around modern northern Utah and Colorado

facts.statement: Sampson and colleagues described Kosmoceratops in 2010, viewing it as strong support for the idea of dinosaur provinces.
facts.quote: Sampson and colleagues viewed this as the strongest support for the idea of dinosaur "provinces" in their 2010 description.

facts.statement: In 2016, Campbell and colleagues reclassified specimen CMN 8801 as Chasmosaurus and argued that Kosmoceratops was restricted to southern Laramidia.
facts.quote: In 2016, Campbell and colleagues assigned CMN 8801 back to Chasmosaurus, and supported the idea that Kosmoceratops was restricted to southern Laramidia.

facts.statement: The genus Kosmoceratops was established by Sampson and colleagues in 2010.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Sampson et al., 2010

facts.statement: The species Kosmoceratops richardsoni was named by Sampson and colleagues in 2010.
facts.quote: species_authority: Sampson et al., 2010

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops lived during the Upper Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cretácico Superior

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops is classified within the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
facts.quote: subfamilia: Chasmosaurinae

facts.statement: Fossils of Kosmoceratops were discovered in the Kaiparowits Formation of the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in 2006 and 2007.
facts.quote: Las muestras fueron descubiertas en la formación Kaiparowits del Monumento Nacional Grand Staircase-Escalante en 2006 y 2007

facts.statement: The specific name honors Scott Richardson, who found the specimens.
facts.quote: El nombre específico honra a Scott Richardson, quien encontró los especímenes

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 75 million years ago in the Campanian stage, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 75 millones de años, en el Campaniense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops had an estimated length of 4.5 meters and a weight of 1.2 tons.
facts.quote: Kosmoceratops tenía una longitud estimada de 4,5 metros y un peso de 1,2 toneladas

facts.statement: With fifteen well-developed horns and horn-like structures, Kosmoceratops possessed the most ornamented skull of all known dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Con quince cuernos bien desarrollados y estructuras en forma de cuerno, poseía el cráneo más adornado de todos los dinosaurios conocidos

facts.statement: Bone histology studies show that Kosmoceratops grew rapidly and had a high metabolism, similar to modern birds and mammals.
facts.quote: Los estudios de histología ósea muestran que Kosmoceratops creció rápidamente y tuvo un metabolismo elevado, similar a las aves y mamíferos modernos

facts.statement: It had long rows of main teeth forming complex cutting batteries containing hundreds of teeth behind a toothless beak.
facts.quote: Tenía largas hileras de dientes principales que formaban complejas baterías de corte que contenían cientos de dientes detrás de un pico, sin dientes

facts.statement: The frill of Kosmoceratops was more extreme than that of Vagaceratops, with a width approximately double its length.
facts.quote: El volante de Kosmoceratops fue más extremo que el de Vagaceratops, su ancho era aproximadamente el doble de su longitud

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops was a chasmosaurine ceratopsid.
facts.quote: Kosmoceratops era un ceratópsido chasmosaurinido

facts.statement: The functions of ceratopsian frills and horns, including display, combat, and species recognition, are debated.
facts.quote: Se han debatido las funciones de los volantes y cuernos ceratopsianos, incluida la visualización, el combate y el reconocimiento de especies

facts.statement: The environment was dominated by wetlands and supported diverse fauna, including the chasmosaurine Utahceratops.
facts.quote: Este ambiente estaba dominado por humedales y sostenía una fauna diversa, incluyendo dinosaurios como el chasmosaurinido Utahceratops

facts.statement: An interpretation suggesting Kosmoceratops in the south was more closely related to geographically separated Vagaceratops in the north has been challenged.
facts.quote: esta interpretación sugiere que Kosmoceratops en el sur estaba más estrechamente relacionado con la geografía Vagaceratops separados en el norte, pero esto ha sido impugnado

facts.statement: A skull from Alberta was initially assigned to Kosmoceratops in 2014 but was later reclassified as Chasmosaurus in 2016.
facts.quote: CMN 8801, un cráneo de Alberta que fue asignado a Kosmoceratops sp. en 2014 pero asignado de nuevo a Chasmosaurus en 2016

facts.statement: Researchers debate whether a specific skull is more closely related to Kosmoceratops or Chasmosaurus.
facts.quote: Los investigadores debaten si estaba más estrechamente relacionado con Kosmoceratops o Chasmosaurus

facts.statement: A phylogenetic analysis by Mallon and colleagues in 2016 placed Kosmoceratops within a specific clade of ceratopsians.
facts.quote: El siguiente cladograma se basa en el análisis de 2016 de Mallon y colegas

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops belongs to the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Chasmosaurinae

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops is classified in the family Ceratopsidae.
facts.quote: Family: Ceratopsidae

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops is a member of the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: Kosmoceratops lived during the Campanian stage, between 83.6 and 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Only two fossil occurrences of Kosmoceratops have been recorded in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 2

facts.statement: Scientists debate whether ceratopsian horns and frills were used for fighting predators, species recognition, or temperature control.
facts.quote: Se han debatido las posibles funciones de los cuernos y volantes ceratopsianos, incluida la lucha contra los depredadores, el reconocimiento de especies y el control de la temperatura

facts.statement: In 2013, David E. Hone and Darren Naish criticized the species recognition hypothesis, noting that no existing animal uses such structures primarily for that purpose.
facts.quote: En 2013, los paleontólogos David E. Hone y Darren Naish criticaron la "hipótesis del reconocimiento de especies", argumentando que ningún animal existente utiliza tales estructuras principalmente para el reconocimiento de especies

facts.statement: Research suggests the increasing complexity of ceratopsian ornaments may be a byproduct of Cope's Rule, which links body size increase with evolutionary time.
facts.quote: Los autores encontraron que la complejidad de los ornamentos aumentó con el tamaño del cuerpo, lo que sugiere que la evolución de la complejidad de los ornamentos fue un subproducto de la regla de Cope
